title: Quarkus support: quarkus-openid-ssf 0.2.0 is built on easyssf
body:
The Quarkiverse extension quarkus-openid-ssf 0.2.0 is on Maven Central as io.quarkiverse.openid-ssf:quarkus-openid-ssf-receiver:0.2.0. Its protocol code is replaced by easyssf 0.1.0: SET verification, metadata discovery, stream management, push and poll delivery, de-duplication and the OAuth2 client credentials. The extension keeps what is Quarkus, the configuration, the CDI wiring, the Vert.x push route, the poll scheduler, the token providers, Micrometer, the Dev UI and native image support. The getting started guide has a Quarkus tab.

New with the release:

  • Built and tested against Quarkus 3.27 LTS.
  • Several transmitters per application, a JDBC de-duplication store over the default datasource and a SmallRye Health check, the same features the Spring Boot starter has.
  • The strict SET validation of easyssf: the top-level sub_id of SSF 1.0 with a legacy mode for older transmitters, critical subject members, HTTPS for the transmitter.
  • The four receiver plans of the OpenID conformance suite run against the extension, and two new examples, a resource server and a web application with Keycloak, mirror the Spring Boot examples.

0.2.0 changes the event handler SPI, the push and poll semantics and the metric names of the extension; the release notes walk through the migration from 0.1.x.

title: easyssf 0.1.0, the first release
body:
easyssf 0.1.0 is on Maven Central: org.easyssf:easyssf-receiver-spring-boot-starter:0.1.0 for Spring Boot 4.1 applications, easyssf-receiver for everything else, easyssf-receiver-jdbc for the database-backed stores and easyssf-test for the tests of your own receiver.

What the release contains:

  • A receiver for the OpenID Shared Signals Framework 1.0 with push and poll delivery, stream management and verification, de-duplication and the CAEP session and token revocation handlers; it passes the four receiver plans of the OpenID conformance suite (SSF 1.0 and the CAEP Interop Profile, push and poll).
  • Strict by default: SETs need the top-level sub_id of SSF 1.0 (a legacy mode accepts older transmitters), critical subject members a receiver does not understand are rejected, transmitters must use HTTPS, and only asymmetric signature algorithms are accepted.
  • Several transmitters per application, issuer-scoped revocations, a health indicator and Micrometer metrics for Spring Boot.
  • The framework-free modules are Java modules; every artifact is signed, ships a CycloneDX SBOM and a self-contained POM.

The release notes list the changes; SECURITY.md has the signing key.

title: Several transmitters per application
body:
A receiver can now take events from more than one transmitter, several Keycloak realms for instance. The settings at easyssf.receiver.* keep configuring the one transmitter most applications have; further ones go under easyssf.receiver.transmitters.<name>.*, each complete on its own.

  • The issuer of a SET selects the transmitter that verifies it, so one push endpoint serves all of them, each authenticating with its own header. Polled transmitters are polled independently.
  • The beans of the single-transmitter setup are unchanged; the new SsfTransmitters bean holds every transmitter by name and issuer, and SsfTransmitterCustomizer beans adjust them before they are built.
  • Metrics carry a transmitter tag, and the health indicator lists every transmitter.
  • For receivers without Spring Boot: SsfTransmitter, SsfTransmitters and the issuer-routing verifier are in easyssf-receiver.

title: Full subject identifiers, a health indicator and test support
body:
A round of changes after a review of the API, before the first release.

  • Subjects as RFC 9493 defines them. SsfSubjectIdentifier represents every format, and SsfSubject exposes all members of a complex subject. The shortcuts for user, session and email are unchanged. Matching an iss_sub identifier now requires the issuer as well as the subject, and token revocations are scoped to the issuer of the token.
  • HTTPS for the transmitter. The issuer and every endpoint in its metadata must use HTTPS; loopback addresses may use HTTP for local development, and easyssf.receiver.allow-insecure-http lifts the rule for test setups, with a warning at startup.
  • Your own event type aliases, registered in configuration or with SsfEventTypes.registerAlias, without redefining the built-in ones.
  • Typed transmitter metadata: specVersion(), deliveryMethodsSupported(), criticalSubjectMembers(), authorizationSchemes() and defaultSubjects().
  • Immutable value objects. Tokens, subjects, stream configurations and metadata copy what they are given and cannot be changed afterwards.
  • Health indicator easyssf for Spring Boot Actuator: whether the transmitter was reached, the stream is registered and the last poll succeeded, without calling the transmitter.
  • easyssf-test: the transmitter the easyssf tests use, as a module for the tests of your own receiver.
  • Every artifact ships with a CycloneDX SBOM, a self-contained POM and an automatic module name.

The schema of the EASYSSF_REVOCATION table gained an ISSUER column; nothing was released yet, so there is no migration.

title: Welcome to easyssf.org
body:
easyssf has a home. The project is a Java library and a Spring Boot 4.1 starter that turn an application into a receiver for the OpenID Shared Signals Framework: it verifies Security Event Tokens, rejects the access tokens and ends the sessions a CAEP event revokes, and hands every event to your own handlers.

Where things stand:

  • The receiver library has no framework dependencies; the Spring Boot starter covers the servlet stack, resource servers and OIDC clients.
  • Tested against the SSF transmitter of Keycloak 26.8 and the receiver test plans of the OpenID conformance suite.
  • The code is experimental and not yet published to Maven Central. Build it from source with ./mvnw install.

The source is on GitHub.
